_meta.comment: Hand-authored tips overriding the converter's auto-generated tips for D3. Same conventions as d1.json / d2.json.

d3_001: Trap is B 'project steering committee' — provides oversight and direction, but doesn't review individual deliverables for fitness.
Trap is C 'senior management' — approves resources and major milestones, but doesn't review deliverables operationally.
Trap is D 'QA staff' — reviews against quality standards, but the user owns whether the system meets THEIR needs.
User management owns the system being built. They alone can confirm 'this deliverable matches what we asked for'.
d3_002: Trap is A 'Gantt chart' — visualizes the schedule but doesn't help PRIORITIZE based on dependency criticality.
Trap is B 'earned value analysis' — measures progress vs plan, doesn't determine the timeline.
Trap is D 'function point analysis' — sizes the work, doesn't sequence it.
PERT identifies the critical path — the sequence of dependent activities determining minimum project duration. That's how priority and timeline get set.
d3_003: Trap is B 'time management' — the time issue is a SYMPTOM; the cause is functionality exceeding requirements.
Trap is C 'risk management' — should have caught the scope expansion but isn't the root cause discipline.
Trap is D 'procurement' — unrelated to scope creep.
Implementing functionality beyond requirements = scope expansion = scope management failure. Time and cost overruns are downstream consequences.
d3_004: Trap is B 'system configuration' — too technical for end users; potential security risk.
Trap is C 'program logic specification' — programmer's territory; users can't validate logic, only outcomes.
Trap is D 'performance tuning' — technical, requires deep system knowledge.
End users excel at output testing because they know what 'right' looks like for their job. Comparing inputs to expected outputs is squarely within user competence.
d3_005: Trap is A 'data accuracy controls' — production data is already accurate.
Trap is B 'inaccurate test results' — production data tends to make tests MORE realistic, not less.
Trap is C 'hardware not identical' — environment concern, not data concern.

Production data in a test environment with weaker access controls = confidentiality breach risk. Programmers may have test environment access they wouldn't have in production — exposing sensitive data.
d3_006: Trap is A 'cost savings' — parallel running is EXPENSIVE (running two systems for 30 days).
Trap is B 'hardware compatibility' — verified earlier in the project, not by parallel run.
Trap is D 'increased resiliency' — true side effect but not the primary advantage of parallel running.
Parallel running compares new system output to known-good old system output. That's the strongest assurance the new system works correctly — by direct comparison.
d3_007: Trap is A 'alpha testing' — early-stage testing, internal only.
Trap is B 'white box testing' — code-aware testing during development, not user testing.
Trap is C 'regression testing' — validates that fixes didn't break other things, not user-facing.
Beta testing = late-stage, real users in real conditions. Last verification before release.
d3_008: Trap is A 'acceptance testing' — final user-facing test, not architectural.
Trap is B 'system testing' — full system integration, but architectural design is tested earlier.
Trap is D 'unit testing' — module-level, doesn't test architecture.
Integration testing exercises the architectural design — how components connect. Unit-tested modules combined according to design = integration test.
d3_009: ITF runs test transactions WITH live data using a fictitious entity. Tests can run anytime without separate test infrastructure.
Trap is A 'no need to review transaction source' — false; auditor still needs source verification.
Trap is C 'validates application AND ensures correct operation' — too broad; ITF is a specific testing approach, not a guarantee.
Trap is D 'no test data needed' — false; test transactions are still required, just integrated with live processing.
d3_010: Trap is A 'undocumented project change approvals' — process concern, recoverable.
Trap is C 'incomplete testing of standard functionality' — manageable through additional UAT.
Trap is D 'duplicating existing payroll permissions' — operational concern, configurable.
Faulty data migration in payroll = wrong paychecks. Direct human/financial/legal consequence. Highest-impact risk in the scenario.
d3_011: Trap is A 'advise on application controls adoption' — designing controls compromises auditor independence.
Trap is B 'provide future licensing estimates' — auditor doesn't do project budgeting.
Trap is C 'recommend efficiency improvements' — operational consulting, compromises independence.
Reviewing test case documentation is audit-appropriate: assess completeness without designing or operating controls. Stays within the audit role.
d3_012: Trap is A 'UAT' — happens before implementation, not during postimplementation review.
Trap is C 'activate audit trails' — should already be active; not a postimplementation activity.
Trap is D 'update EA diagrams' — documentation hygiene, not the primary postimplementation question.
Postimplementation review answers: did this investment deliver promised value? ROI analysis re-evaluates the original business case against actual outcomes.
d3_013: Trap is B 'restrict to functional requirements' — ignores nonfunctional (performance, security, usability) which are equally important.
Trap is C 'automated tests with scripting' — useful tactically but doesn't ensure coverage of important areas.
Trap is D 'retest only defect fixes' — leaves untouched code untested; coverage gap.
Risk-based testing: use frequency and importance to allocate scarce test time to highest-risk requirements. Maximizes risk reduction per test hour.
d3_014: Trap is A 'reliable products guaranteed' — too strong; CMM measures process, not product reliability.
Trap is B 'efficiency improved' — possible outcome, not what CMM measures.
Trap is C 'security designed' — separate concern from process maturity.
CMM evaluates whether the dev organization has STABLE, PREDICTABLE processes. That's the entire point: process maturity, not specific outcomes.
d3_015: Trap is A/D 'recalculations / reconciliations' — detective controls; don't prevent input errors.
Trap is C 'run-to-run totals' — detect processing errors, not input errors.
Limit checks operate at input time, rejecting invalid values before they enter the system. Preventive control closest to the source.
d3_016: Trap is B 'billing cost allocation' — financial concern, addressable post-rollout.
Trap is C 'multiple application owners' — common in shared apps; manageable through governance.
Trap is D 'no training program' — user adoption issue, addressable.
Without process owners, there's no accountability for operations, monitoring, or authorization decisions. Foundational governance gap that affects all departments.
d3_017: Trap is B 'security standards met' — checked later in the acquisition process.
Trap is C 'users involved in implementation' — implementation phase concern, not initial acquisition.
Trap is D 'meets all user functionality' — too broad; may not be required and may exceed budget.
Acquisition starts with a clear business case approved by management. Without that, the entire acquisition lacks business justification — everything else is moot.
d3_018: Trap is A 'noncompliance with software licensing' — SaaS reduces this risk; vendor manages licensing.
Trap is C 'higher cost from licensing' — SaaS typically REDUCES total cost.
Trap is D 'higher cost for compatible hardware' — SaaS doesn't require hardware updates.
SaaS depends entirely on Internet connectivity. Performance and availability follow Internet quality, not the customer's local infrastructure. Most likely day-to-day risk.
d3_019: Trap is A 'changing user needs' — manageable through change control; not the most common cause.
Trap is B 'inaccurate growth forecast' — capacity issue, addressable through scaling.
Trap is C 'hardware concurrency limits' — technical, addressable.
Inadequate user participation in requirements = systems built to assumed needs, not actual needs. Most fundamental and most common failure mode.
d3_020: Trap is A 'function point analysis' — sizes the work, doesn't directly estimate duration.
Trap is C 'rapid application development' — methodology, doesn't estimate.
Trap is D 'object-oriented system development' — design approach, doesn't estimate.
PERT estimates duration using best/worst/normal scenarios. Specifically designed for project duration estimation under uncertainty.
d3_021: Trap is A 'CMM' — assesses process maturity, doesn't help select projects.
Trap is C 'configuration management' — controls software/hardware versions, not project selection.
Trap is D 'PMBOK' — body of knowledge for managing projects, not selecting them.
Portfolio management is purpose-built for project prioritization across the org — comparing initiatives by business value and risk. That's what enables strategic project selection.
d3_022: Trap is A 'prevent further changes' — too restrictive; changes are valuable when justified.
Trap is B 'design completion point' — descriptive, not the rationale for the freeze.
Trap is D 'project management control' — outcome but not the primary purpose.
Stop point exists to FORCE cost-benefit evaluation of late changes. Without it, scope creep destroys the original business case.
d3_023: Trap is A 'iterative nature' — characteristic of prototyping, not the change-control complication.
Trap is C 'emphasis on reports and screens' — focus area, not change-control issue.
Trap is D 'lack of integrated tools' — tooling gap, addressable.
Prototyping moves fast — requirements and design change session by session. Documentation and approval can't keep up, undermining traditional change control.
d3_024: Trap is A 'project progressing as planned' — superficially true (on time, under budget) but ignores team strain.
Trap is B 'overtime cost tracking' — accounting concern, not project plan concern.
Trap is C 'programmers slow to earn overtime' — unfair speculation about staff.
Massive unplanned overtime = the project plan was wrong (under-estimated). The plan is meeting deadlines through team burnout, not realistic scheduling. Investigate.
d3_025: Trap is B 'production data introduced' — already addressed (sensitive data was scrubbed).
Trap is C 'specialized training' — operational concern, not test data concern.
Trap is D 'over budget' — generic project risk, not test deck specific.
Production data covers normal cases but may MISS edge cases, error conditions, and rare scenarios. Test functionality won't be fully exercised.
d3_026: Trap is A 'TCO' — important but a SUBSET of the ROI calculation.
Trap is B 'resources for implementation' — input to the cost side, not the full picture.
Trap is D 'security cost and complexity' — one cost component.
Business case = ROI = full benefit/cost picture. ROI is what justifies the acquisition; everything else is an input to ROI.
d3_027: Trap is A 'no right-to-audit clause' — concerning but addressable through other assurance mechanisms.
Trap is C 'no source code escrow' — addressable through contractual update.
Trap is D 'no change management coverage' — operational concern, can be added to contract.
No business case = the outsourcing decision wasn't strategically evaluated. Risk, value, alternatives, and exit strategies were never assessed. Foundational governance failure.
d3_028: Trap is B 'don't reduce productivity' — operational concern, secondary to risk mitigation purpose.
Trap is C 'minimized cost analysis' — backwards; controls should match risk, not minimize cost.
Trap is D 'detective or corrective' — false dichotomy; preventive controls are also valid.
Controls exist to mitigate identified RISK. Controls without a corresponding risk are wasteful; controls misaligned to risk are ineffective. Risk drives the requirement.
d3_029: Trap is A 'console log' — system-level, doesn't capture user transaction details.
Trap is C 'automated suspense file' — captures errors only, misses successful unauthorized input.
Trap is D 'user error report' — captures user-reported errors, not unauthorized actions.
Transaction journal captures every transaction with user attribution. Comparing journal entries to authorized sources surfaces unauthorized inputs.
d3_030: Trap is A 'prototyping methodology' — one factor, but methodology choice can succeed in good environments and fail in bad ones.
Trap is B 'external compliance' — important but doesn't drive overall success.
Trap is D 'software reengineering' — technique, not environment.
Organizational environment includes: business-IT alignment, process maturity, change control discipline, governance. Same project in different environments has wildly different outcomes.
d3_031: Trap is A/B 'central site after / during application run' — already past the cost of bad transmission; data quality should be enforced earlier.
Trap is C 'remote site after transmission' — paradoxical; if you're going to validate at the remote site, do it BEFORE wasting bandwidth.
Validate at the source, before transmission. Catches errors with minimum cost — no wasted bandwidth, no central-site processing of bad data, no later cleanup.
d3_032: Trap is A/D 'IT budget / investment plan' — financial constraints, derived from business plan.
Trap is B 'existing IT environment' — current state, doesn't drive future selection.
Project portfolio prioritization is a strategic exercise. The business plan is the ultimate filter — projects must serve business strategy first; budget and environment are constraints, not drivers.
d3_033: Trap is A 'meets customer requirements' — that's UAT or system testing.
Trap is B 'operate in target environment' — that's sociability/deployment testing.
Trap is C 'development standards maintained' — quality assurance, not regression.
Regression testing's specific job: verify that changes didn't BREAK previously-working functionality. Re-running prior tests catches new errors introduced by changes.
d3_034: Trap is A 'validation controls' — catch invalid input but don't track totals end-to-end.
Trap is B 'internal credibility checks' — sniff-test for plausibility, doesn't catch loss.
Trap is C 'clerical procedures' — manual, error-prone, doesn't scale.
Automated systems balancing: total inputs = total outputs. Discrepancy = lost transaction, automatically flagged for investigation. Best for multi-source/multi-format processing.
d3_035: Trap is B 'regression test failures' — possible side effect, not the primary scope-change concern.
Trap is C 'users not agreeing' — adoption issue, secondary.
Trap is D 'team skills' — capability concern, secondary.
Scope changes shift duration and cost — that's why impact studies exist. Without one, the project commits to changes whose true cost is unknown.
d3_036: Trap is B 'features not extensively documented' — agile prefers minimal documentation; this is by design.
Trap is C 'continual re-planning' — agile core practice; iterative re-planning is expected.
Trap is D 'team manages own resources' — agile self-organization principle.
Agile's non-negotiable: each iteration produces SHIPPABLE code. Proof-of-concept and unfinished code violate the iteration principle and undermine agile's value proposition.
d3_037: Trap is A 'range check' — catches values outside allowed range, not order errors.
Trap is C 'validity check' — catches invalid values, not transposition.
Trap is D 'duplicate check' — catches duplicates, different problem.
Check digit is mathematically computed from the original digits. Transposing digits changes the computed value, exposing the error. Designed for transposition/transcription detection.
d3_038: Trap is A 'user feedback documented' — useful but doesn't validate system controls.
Trap is B 'cost benefits measured' — financial review, secondary in two months.
Trap is D 'subsequent change requests' — quality indicator, indirect.
Postimplementation control review tests whether built-in controls are working as designed. Management's 'went well' assumption needs INDEPENDENT verification — that's the auditor's value-add.
d3_039: Trap is A 'sign-off delays' — process inconvenience, downstream of scope creep.
Trap is B 'software integrity violations' — different control problem.
Trap is D 'inadequate controls' — possible but indirect.
Without baselining, requirements continue evolving without formal cost-benefit evaluation. Result: SCOPE CREEP — the project keeps growing past its original justification.
d3_040: Trap is A 'user access' — important but follows architectural understanding.
Trap is B 'change request process' — process review, comes after understanding flow.
Trap is C 'reconciliation controls' — placement depends on data flow understanding.
Data flow diagram first. Until the auditor understands HOW data moves between components, they can't evaluate WHERE controls should sit or whether they're effective.
d3_041: Trap is A 'compatibility testing' — late-cycle technical concern.
Trap is B 'gap analysis' — useful but premature without process verification.
Trap is C 'licensing review' — operational follow-up.
Acquisition deviating from procedures = procedure compliance issue first. Verify whether the deviation was authorized before evaluating the technical merits.
d3_042: Trap is A 'system testing' — earlier stage; failures here can be fixed before deployment.
Trap is C 'integration testing' — earlier; modules can be reworked.
Trap is D 'unit testing' — earliest; cheapest to fix.
Acceptance testing is the LAST checkpoint before go-live. Failure here delays deployment and forces emergency rework, often disrupting business plans tied to the launch date.
d3_043: Trap is B 'increased security' — possible but standardization isn't security-driven.
Trap is C 'reduced infrastructure investment' — opposite; standardization may require initial investment.
Trap is D 'no testing of future changes' — overstated; testing is still required.
Standardization reduces operational complexity: fewer platforms to support, common tooling, easier patching/monitoring. Cost-effectiveness is the most direct benefit.
d3_044: Trap is B 'transaction speed' — important but warehouses prioritize query/analysis, not transaction speed.
Trap is C 'data volatility' — characteristic, not design driver.
Trap is D 'system vulnerability' — security concern, not design factor.
Metadata describes what's in the warehouse — without it, queries can't reliably interpret the data. Quality metadata is foundational for analytical use.
d3_045: Trap is A 'test environment with test data' — small-volume data won't reveal capacity issues.
Trap is B 'production environment with live workloads' — risk of breaking production.
Trap is D 'production with test data' — production environment good but test data won't stress it.
Stress testing's purpose: confirm system handles real production load. Use a test environment (safe) with production-realistic workloads (meaningful).
d3_046: Trap is A 'tracking completion' — measurement, not design driver.
Trap is B 'optimize UAT cost' — secondary benefit.
Trap is C 'minimize requirements gap' — outcome of process owner involvement, not the reason for it.
Process owners know the business processes the system must support. Without them, design risks being technically correct but business-misaligned.
d3_047: Trap is A 'lab testing phase' — too late; system is being tested.
Trap is B 'before user acceptance' — also too late; testing already happening.
Trap is D 'implementation phase' — far too late.
IS auditor reviewing control specifications during requirements gathering = maximum influence with minimum disruption. Earlier = cheaper to fix.
d3_048: Trap is B 'after early planning' — vague; planning IS where phases get defined.
Trap is C 'during work, based on risk' — emergent planning misses early phase definition.
Trap is D 'after risk identification + auditor recommendations' — too constrained; project planning shouldn't wait on auditors.
Phases and deliverables defined upfront enables tracking, resource allocation, and milestone management. Without early definition, projects drift without measurable progress.
d3_049: Trap is A 'cost benefits' — relevant but doesn't address WHY phase 1 went over.
Trap is B 'control balances' — operational verification, not the strategic learning.
Trap is D 'system objectives achieved' — success measurement, not learning.
Phase 1's problems likely affect phase 2+. Reviewing impact of those changes gives forward-looking insight — what to mitigate before next phase repeats the same mistakes.
d3_050: Trap is A 'multiple software versions' — version control issue, manageable.
Trap is B 'source/object code mismatch' — change control issue, eventually surfaces.
Trap is D 'programming errors' — software quality concern, present in all systems.
Incorrect parameters at go-live = immediate failure or vulnerability. Common with packages because parameters are often invisible until exercised in production.
d3_051: Trap is A 'strong internal controls' — opposite; prototyping often UNDER-emphasizes controls.
Trap is C 'simpler change control' — opposite; change control is HARDER with prototyping.
Trap is D 'no extra functions' — opposite; prototyping invites scope creep.
Prototyping's actual benefit: rapid feedback loops with users → faster delivery, better fit, lower wrong-system risk. Quality and control are tradeoffs, not advantages.
d3_052: Trap is B 'harden the network' — operational outcome, narrow.
Trap is C 'highlight importance to management' — political objective, secondary.
Trap is D 'employee awareness' — training outcome, secondary.
Post-incident review's PRIMARY purpose: improve internal controls. Each incident teaches what controls failed; the review converts that into control improvements.
d3_053: Trap is A 'all transaction types included' — depends on what live data was sanitized.
Trap is B 'every error condition tested' — live data won't necessarily exercise all errors.
Trap is C 'no special routines for results' — incorrect; results still need analysis.
Sanitized live data preserves real-world transaction patterns — frequencies, distributions, edge cases. More realistic than synthetic test data, safer than raw production.
d3_054: Trap is A 'users prefer contrived data' — possible but not the audit concern.
Trap is C 'error handling not proven' — testing concern, not the primary audit concern.
Trap is D 'full functionality not tested' — coverage concern, secondary.
Production data in test environments without sanitization = sensitive data exposure to people who normally wouldn't have access. Privacy/regulatory risk.
d3_055: Trap is A 'cost-effectiveness' — financial test, not parallel testing's purpose.
Trap is B 'unit and system testing' — earlier-stage tests, not parallel.
Trap is C 'program interface errors' — technical concern, addressable in unit/integration test.
Parallel testing runs old and new systems with the same data. Output comparison reveals whether the new system meets user requirements — by direct comparison to the known-good old system.
d3_056: Trap is A 'rules' — production rule systems, different structure.
Trap is C 'semantic nets' — graph-based knowledge representation, not questionnaire-based.
Trap is D 'dataflow diagrams' — process modeling tool, not knowledge representation.
Decision trees encode 'if X then Y else Z' branching as a tree. Questionnaires walking users through choices map directly to this structure.
d3_057: Trap is A 'interface errors detected earlier' — that's TOP-DOWN's advantage.
Trap is B 'confidence achieved earlier' — top-down builds confidence in the architecture earlier.
Trap is D 'major functions tested earlier' — also top-down.
Bottom-up tests atomic units first — programs, modules. Critical-module errors surface immediately, before they cascade through the system. Defect cost lower when caught early at unit level.
d3_058: Trap is A 'feasibility study' — too early; user requirements not yet defined.
Trap is C 'implementation planning' — too late; UAT plans should be ready by then.
Trap is D 'postimplementation review' — way too late; UAT happens before implementation.
Requirements definition is when users articulate what they need. UAT plans get authored alongside, asking 'how will we test that requirement?' Same time, same conversation.
d3_059: Trap is B 'improves performance' — abstraction can ADD overhead, not improve performance.
Trap is C 'enhances control effectiveness' — control depends on design, not paradigm.
Trap is D 'speeds up SDLC' — initial OO design takes longer; speed comes later via reuse.
Object-oriented design's signature benefit: encapsulation enables modules to be reused across projects. That's where the long-term productivity gains come from.
d3_060: Trap is A 'encryption algorithm format' — implementation detail, downstream of feasibility.
Trap is B 'detailed internal control procedures' — also detailed; feasibility is high-level.
Trap is D 'trusted third-party agreement' — operational detail.
Communication protocols drive feasibility — they determine hardware/software requirements, costs, and integration complexity. Without protocol clarity, the feasibility study can't estimate.
d3_061: Trap is A 'finish writing user manuals' — documentation; can follow implementation.
Trap is C 'add last-minute enhancements' — exactly what to AVOID under time pressure.
Trap is D 'documented and reviewed code' — process discipline; secondary to functional verification.
UAT is the only test that confirms the system actually works for users. Skipping UAT under time pressure = high risk of go-live failure. Documentation can wait; functional validation can't.
d3_062: Trap is A 'pre-BPR flowcharts' — historical context, not the audit subject.
Trap is C 'BPR project plans' — process documentation, not control implementation.
Trap is D 'continuous improvement plans' — forward-looking, doesn't validate current controls.
Post-BPR flowcharts show the NEW process. Auditor checks that key controls were preserved or properly redesigned in the new process — the actual deliverable to validate.
d3_063: Trap is A 'PERT' — estimates project DURATION, not size of effort.
Trap is C 'source lines of code' — old technique, doesn't scale to complex systems.
Trap is D 'white box testing' — testing technique, not estimation.
Function point analysis quantifies system size by counting inputs, outputs, queries, files, and interfaces. Specifically designed for development effort estimation.
d3_064: Trap is A 'users manage acceptance testing' — appropriate; users own UAT.
Trap is C 'not all functions in initial release' — phased delivery is acceptable.
Trap is D 'prototyping for requirements confirmation' — valid technique.
Quality plan defines how the project ensures deliverables meet quality standards. Without it, quality is undefined and unmeasurable. Critical contractual deliverable.
d3_065: Trap is A 'discuss a single solution' — premature; alternatives should be considered.
Trap is B 'consider security controls' — important but a SUBSET of feasibility.
Trap is D 'consult audit department' — secondary input.
Feasibility study + cost-benefit demonstrates the proposal CAN work AND IS worth doing. That's what management needs to make an informed decision.
